cells.tense: You're at the table with your own sense of what's right, and it's reading clean today.
cells.ask: Before you settle one split — a bill, a chore, a round — let the tab sit open in your head for an hour and let your own numbers come up on their own. What it gives back is a call you hand over once and no longer need to check.
cells.core:
You catch the imbalance early — the half-second tightness when the numbers are off, when someone's carrying more than they're being credited for. It isn't loud, it isn't usually welcome, and it tends to be right. That private sense keeps the books straight when nobody else is looking.

Because the sense is steady, the pull is to settle everything the instant it registers. The next move worth trying isn't a louder fairness — it's letting one tab sit open for an hour before you settle it, so the call has room to arrive from somewhere other than the reflex. What that gets you is a fair call you don't have to keep rechecking.
cells.sheetLine: You know what's fair before anyone says it, and your call tends to hold.
cells.verb: Weighing what's fair before anyone else says a word.
cells.place: Standing where you can see what you actually want, and pulled toward it.

cells.tense: You're already running the math on a reckoning that hasn't arrived, tallying debts nobody handed you.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've been circling as unfair, out loud or on a page, and finish the sentence with 'and here's what's owed back.' What it gives back is the difference between a debt that's yours and a debt you've been carrying for someone else.
cells.core:
Pointed at real ledgers, this sense is just useful — you catch the imbalance in a room before anyone else does. When it tilts, the same sense starts drafting verdicts nobody asked for. You track accounts against a court date that keeps not arriving, which means you're rarely only in the room you're in. Wanting to be on the right side of fair does a lot of the scoring.

Sensing a debt and being sentenced to carry one aren't the same thing. Pick one thing you've been circling as unfair, and finish the sentence 'and here's what's owed back' — out loud or on a page. The point isn't to agree you owe it; it's to see which debts are yours and which ones you signed for.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping score against a reckoning that hasn't come.
cells.verb: Weighing what's fair before anyone else says a word.
cells.place: Standing where you can see what you actually want, and pulled toward it.

cells.tense: The sense went quiet a while back, and you've been living as if the last word on fair had already been said.
cells.ask: Open one envelope or statement you haven't looked at in a while and read it only — no paying, no deciding. What it gives back is proof the math still works in your own hands.
cells.core:
In an open stretch, fairness moves both ways: you register what's owed, you say so, and the give-and-take settles without endless auditing. What isn't happening right now is the catching. You stopped flinching when the bill came, missed the phrasing a friend used asking for a favor, didn't notice the chore that quietly moved to your side of the counter. Nothing was closed out. It just stopped being handled.

Rebuilding it won't come from deciding to care more about fairness. It comes from contact with actual numbers in your own hand — open one statement you've been avoiding and read it, nothing else. Watch what the figures do in your chest, and that watching is where the sense picks its instrument back up.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped reading the numbers, and the sense went with them.
cells.verb: Weighing what's fair before anyone else says a word.
cells.place: Standing where you can see what you actually want, and pulled toward it.

cells.tense: You're weighing what's fair in every room you walk into — you've just been filing it under something else.
cells.ask: Say one plain sentence about a situation you've been calling 'practical' — first thought, no edits. What it gives back is hearing the fairness land as the sentence you just said rather than as background noise.
cells.core:
The compass is on. It's the small shift in mood when a name gets dropped from credit, the instant change in how you move around someone who's been unfair, the pause before you agree to a favor — and all of it is going on under labels like 'just being realistic' or 'practical.' Your fairness is doing real work in the room. You're just not claiming the call as yours.

Nothing needs installing. The labels have taken the sentence, and the compass needs the verb back. Pick one situation you've been carrying as plain practical, and say a single sentence about it — first thought, out loud or on a page. You'll hear the fairness in your own voice, which is different from knowing it's in there.
cells.sheetLine: You're already weighing fair against unfair — you're just calling it 'being practical.'
cells.verb: Weighing what's fair before anyone else says a word.
cells.place: Standing where you can see what you actually want, and pulled toward it.

attempts.check: The record gives me the card's mechanism (private fairness-feeling, Body/Fruition/Resonance, number 5) and the seat (aspirational pull), but no facts about how this person thinks, what they've done, or whether any of this is actually what's happening for them. The reader might reasonably say: my fairness feels sharpest exactly when I've been let down, not abstractly — and nothing in the cell contradicts that, since the cell locates the sense rather than narrating an event. The asks (a page of per-heads, one closed account, a statement said once, calling a reaction a wish) stay useful even if my read is wrong, because each one only requires doing a small physical thing today and learning from it, not accepting a diagnosis. One sentence I'd watch is 'you keep the ledger in a currency only you can read' in the Balanced opening — it risks flattering the writer's phrasing more than serving the person standing at the table; I've kept it because it names a real Body/Fruition mechanism (balance-keeping that stays private and never gets cashed out), but if it reads as a performance on the page, cut it and go straight to the split-payment picture.
